title: Ordered and Unordered Lists
summary: Choose ordered or unordered lists based on content meaning.

sketchBlocks.title: Use an unordered list when sequence does not matter
sketchBlocks.bodyMarkdown:
A list groups related items so the browser and reader understand that the items belong together. Use `
    ` when sequence is not important, such as supplies, features, or names. Each item belongs in `
  • `. ```html
    • Notebook
    • Pen
    ``` The bullets are a browser default; the important HTML meaning is that these are related list items. Read this example line by line: the opening `
      ` starts one unordered group. The first `
    • ` creates the Notebook item, the second `
    • ` creates the Pen item, and the closing `
    ` ends the group. The browser may draw bullets, but the HTML structure is what says these values belong to the same unordered set.

sketchBlocks.title: Use an ordered list for a sequence
sketchBlocks.bodyMarkdown:
Use `
    ` when changing the order would change the meaning: instructions, rankings, or steps. ```html
    1. Check in
    2. Find your seat
    3. Open your notebook
    ``` The browser numbers the items because the sequence is part of the content. Read the ordered-list example line by line: `
      ` opens a sequence whose order matters. Each `
    1. ` adds one step: Check in first, Find your seat second, and Open your notebook third. The closing `
    ` finishes the sequence. Moving a list item would change the meaning of the instructions.

sketchBlocks.title: Put list items inside the correct list container
sketchBlocks.bodyMarkdown:
`<ul>` and `<ol>` are containers. Their direct items use `<li>`.

A page can use both list types when different groups have different meanings. Use an unordered list for a set of things and an ordered list for steps.

quizDraft.title: Group the open-house supplies
quizDraft.prompt: Replace the three supply paragraphs with one unordered list. Keep the same three item texts and watch the browser preview show them as one grouped list.
quizDraft.hint: The items belong together, but their order does not matter.

help.concept: An unordered list represents related items whose sequence is not meaningful.
help.hint_1: Wrap the group in a ul element.
help.hint_2: Each supply needs its own li element inside the ul.

quizDraft.title: Choose the list with the right meaning
quizDraft.prompt: A page explains three steps for submitting an assignment. Which element should contain the steps?
quizDraft.hint: Think about whether the sequence matters.

help.hint_2: Use the list container that communicates first, second, third.

quizDraft.title: Identify correct list uses
quizDraft.prompt: Which two statements use list semantics appropriately?
quizDraft.hint: Choose based on content meaning, not decoration.

help.concept: List semantics describe unordered sets or ordered sequences.
help.hint_1: One correct answer describes a set; the other describes steps.
help.hint_2: Ignore choices that use list tags only for appearance or omit the container.

options: Use <ul> for a set of club supplies where order does not matter.
Use <ol> only because you prefer numbers visually.
Use <ol> for instructions that must be followed in sequence.
Place list items directly in <body> without a list container.

quizDraft.title: Build an ordered list
quizDraft.prompt: Arrange the tokens into a valid ordered list with two steps.
quizDraft.hint: The list container surrounds its list items.

help.concept: A valid ordered list opens ol, contains li elements, and closes ol.
help.hint_1: Start with the opening ol tag.
help.hint_2: Both li elements go before the closing ol tag.

quizDraft.title: Complete the list item
quizDraft.prompt: Choose the markup that correctly fills the one missing item inside this unordered list.
quizDraft.hint: Look for the element that represents one item in a list.

help.concept: The li element represents an individual item inside ul or ol.
help.hint_2: Fill the blank with one complete li element.
